source.title: Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets
source.authors: Hao Li; Zheng Xu; Gavin Taylor; Christoph Studer; T. Goldstein

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Uses filter-normalized loss-landscape visualizations to relate minimizer sharpness to generalization and reports how architecture, batch size, optimizer, and width affect test error.
record.gate_note: Cited findings from prior work, including random-label memorization, are not this study's own results. Rows below cover its own CIFAR-10 comparisons and reported sharpness–generalization relationships.
record.test_reason: Own CIFAR-10 results test optimizer differences (V4) and batch-size penalties under fixed epoch budgets (V5). Width comparisons do not establish widening beyond interpolation (V2); visual sharpness versus test error does not establish the magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization-gap relationship in V7. This study is not an original source for V4 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report that filter-normalized visual sharpness correlates with test error, and that architecture and training choices alter landscape geometry. Their dimensionality-reduction caution concerns interpreting apparent convexity; they do not establish V7's quantitative generalization-gap ranking.
record.recipe_differences: Visualizes loss landscapes and compares geometry with test error; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiment or the specific sharpness measure in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, optimizer, weight decay, skip connections, network depth, width, and direction normalization change reported test errors or apparent loss-landscape geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Widening ResNet-56 lowers test error from 5.89% to 5.07%, 4.34%, and 3.93%; the interpolation threshold is not established.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing convolutional width can improve CIFAR-10 test accuracy under a fixed regularized training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Filter-normalized visual flatness qualitatively tracks test error across the displayed architectures and training settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filter-normalized loss-landscape flatness can correlate with test error in these CIFAR-10 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Unnormalized visual sharpness lacks a consistent relationship with test error, and layer normalization has an explicit counterexample.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The apparent relationship between visual loss sharpness and test error depends on direction normalization.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2018), as stated in the paper text.
record.problems: The central sharpness/generalization result is qualitative and based on low-dimensional plots. The paper cautions that dimensionality reduction affects interpretation. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported test errors.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy are cited, not experimentally tested.
Test error as width increases beyond an established zero-training-error threshold under training to convergence without explicit regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks, systematic learning-rate tuning, broader hyperparameter searches, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and a quantified matched-training-performance comparison. Adam uses default beta and epsilon values and SGD's learning-rate schedule; optimizer-specific tuning is not documented.

Language models, the location of the workload-dependent batch threshold, longer training, warmup and learning-rate scaling, and normalization or regularization changes designed to recover large-batch performance.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance measured through training error, its ranking of train–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, and comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples and comparing retraining with random-example removal.

missing.what: Add matched VGG-9 optimizer comparisons at batch 8192: Adam 10.91% versus SGD 11.07% with zero weight decay, and Adam 9.52% versus SGD 10.19% with weight decay 0.0005. These reverse the optimizer ordering seen at batch 128.

record.verdict_notes: Reported test-error numbers match the supplied text. No uncertainty estimates accompany them. Different architectures, omitted benchmarks, or untested recovery recipes alone do not justify limits_scope verdicts. Unnormalized and layer-normalized visualization failures do not challenge the specified magnitude-aware V7 measure.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization are cited from prior work, not tested here.
Uses wide convolutional residual networks, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks; does not identify a width threshold for zero training error.
Does not compare convolutional networks against fully connected networks trained from scratch.
Only CIFAR-10 VGG-9 and ResNet-56 comparisons are reported; the study does not test language benchmarks or broad hyperparameter tuning.
Tests CIFAR-10 image classifiers at fixed epoch counts; does not test language models or the recipe adaptations in the version.

Uses filter-normalized visual sharpness, not a stated quantitative weight-perturbation ranking against norm- and margin-based measures; does not test CIFAR-10/SVHN without augmentation as described in the version.

rows.subject: VGG-9, ResNet and Wide-ResNet models
rows.operation_detail: Compared filter-normalized loss-landscape sharpness with test error across trained minimizers.
rows.measure: Qualitative association between visual sharpness and test error
rows.value: Authors report that visually flatter minimizers consistently correspond to lower test error.
rows.note: This is a qualitative association across the architectures shown; the study warns that the visualizations use dramatic dimensionality reduction.
rows.check: Measures qualitative filter-normalized loss curvature against test error, rather than perturbation tolerance before training error rises against the train–test error gap. The pooled architectures also include substantially different training errors.

rows.subject: VGG-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-plot sharpness under no normalization and layer normalization with test error.
rows.measure: Whether plot sharpness tracks test error
rows.value: Without normalization, plots fail to show consistency between flatness and generalization error.
rows.note: The paper identifies scaling as a source of misleading apparent sharpness.
rows.check: Failure of unnormalized visual sharpness is not failure of V7's magnitude-aware measure. The stated absence applies to this visualization method.

rows.subject: VGG-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-normalized plot sharpness with test error.
rows.measure: Whether plot sharpness tracks test error
rows.baseline: Filter normalization is reported as more accurate than layer normalization.
rows.value: One failing case: a flatter plot has worse generalization error.
rows.note: The text explicitly reports a failure case for layer normalization.
rows.check: The layer-normalized visualization counterexample does not test V7's specified measure or generalization-gap ranking. For the row's own visual association, the particular comparison is reversed.
